title: Naam japo, deeper
hookLine: remembrance as the root of everything else

cards: The morning after a storm, two old trees on one street. One is down across a lawn, its underside lifted into the air, a flat plate of soil and short roots.
The one next to it, just as tall, still stands, missing a few branches. From above the ground they looked the same. The difference was underneath, where nobody could see it.
Yesterday was the branches: honest work, out in the world. Tomorrow, the fruit: sharing. Today is the part underground.

teach.b: Naam japo. Naam is the Name, the word Sikhs use for the presence of the One, not a label but something lived with. Japo means repeat it, remember it, keep it going.
Guru Nanak's own lines show why it sits underneath.

teach.h: BEFORE DAWN, REFLECT ON THE NAME.
teach.b: In the Japji, the morning prayer, he says, in paraphrase: in the ambrosial hours before dawn, reflect on the true Name and its greatness. That's amrit vela, the early hours some Sikhs keep for this.
Remembrance comes first, before the work.
In a hymn in Raga Asa that Sikhs sing in the evening prayer, there's a line short enough to carry: saying it, I live; forgetting it, I die. The Name isn't an extra. It's breath.
And one more picture from the Japji: when hands and feet and body are covered in dirt, water washes them clean; when the mind is stained, it's washed by love of the Name.
So remembering comes before the day, forgetting is a kind of dying, and the mind gets clean the way hands do, by going back to the water again and again.
That's why it's the root. Honest work without it can turn hard. Sharing without it can turn proud.
With it underneath, both have something to stand on when the wind comes. You don't see a root. You only see what it holds up.

how: Sikhs practice naam japo through nitnem, the daily prayers, through simran, repeating Waheguru, and through kirtan; some rise in amrit vela, the hours before dawn, to begin the day with it.

o: write God's name each day as an offering
chant a secret name given only to the initiated
keep remembering the Name, the root under everything

games.q: the root, in Nanak's words: tap the pairs.
p: washed by love of the Name

s: in the Japji, water washes the body, but the mind is washed by love of the Name
the Japji sets the two side by side: dirt on the hands, stain on the mind, and what cleans each.
in the Asa hymn, Nanak says forgetting the Name is a small thing
he puts it as strongly as he can: saying it, I live; forgetting it, I die.
the Japji places reflection on the Name in the hours before dawn
it speaks of the ambrosial hours, amrit vela, for reflecting on the true Name and its greatness.

games.q: you have three things to do today: work honestly, share, and remember the Name. which one does the lesson put underneath the other two?
games.why: remembrance is the root: it comes before the day's work in the Japji, and the other two stand on it.

practice: Think of the next piece of work waiting for you, a task, a call, a sink full of dishes, and before you touch it, go underneath it.
On each breath, rest your attention on the One, however you understand that: if you pray, say Waheguru silently, once in and once out; if you don't, simply notice the breath as something given.

wordCard.voice: Naam japo. Remember the Name and keep remembering it, the part of Guru Nanak's way that sits underneath work and sharing. Today's word.

orig.note: naam is the Name; japo means repeat it, remember it.

carryVoice: Your line: the root. Under the work and the sharing, out of sight, the Name. Rest well.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji Sahib, pauri 4, Ang 2 (in the ambrosial hours, reflect on the true Name and its greatness)
